Development and applications of deep eutectic solvents in different chromatographic techniques
Mohammad Faraz Ahmer¹ · Qasim Ullah²
Received: 27 September 2022 / Accepted: 5 December 2022 / Published online: 9 January 2023 © Akadémiai Kiadó, Budapest, Hungary 2023

**Abstract** Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) being inexpensive, easy to prepare, biocompatible, biodegradable and environmentally benign have aroused as the most propitious greener solvents for designing novel analytical methods of chemical analysis specially covering almost major fields of chromatography. This review article is majorly concerned with the analytical evaluation of DESs as new generation solvents for use as (a) modifier of silica gel surface via silylation reaction to create new stationary phases, (b) mobile phase (or developer) in liquid chromatography and (c) mobile phase additive to improve chromatographic performance. The sequential evolution of DESs has been briefly presented in tabular form since their beginning from the development of choline chloride/urea eutectic mixture in 2003. It has been observed that three more important properties (ionic conductivity, polarity and viscosity) of DESs can be adjusted to the desired level by proper selection of molar composition of hydrogen bond donor and hydrogen bond acceptor and water content. In this review, we present the recent applications of DESs in chromatography covering the period of the last two decades for assessing their suitability as a new class of green solvents.

**Keywords** Deep eutectic solvents · Supercritical fluid chromatography · Counter-current chromatography · Gas chromatography · Capillary electrochromatography · Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES)

# 1 Introduction Organic solvents are volatile and produce a lot of waste, which would be detrimental to the environment and human health. Organic solvents are being replaced by green or less toxic solvents, for example, ILs (ionic liquids) and DESs (deep eutectic solvents) in separation science particularly in chromatography, in the twenty-first century, based on twelve principles of green chemistry. *Abbott et al.* [1] were the first to prepare the deep eutectic phenomenon in the year of 2003. According to the literature review, DESs have been widely employed in different analytical applications including separation techniques. A review on the application of green solvents in thin-layer chromatography (TLC) was recently published by Qasim Ullah et al. [8]. Furthermore, in recent years, DESs have received more attention of researchers, resulting in the arising number of studies appearing in the literature about properties [9–12] and their applications [13–21]. Abbott and coworkers [22] categorized DESs into four groups based on their compositional components as shown in Fig. 2.

According to the literature survey, type III DESs analogs to ILs in terms of physicochemical properties have been commonly investigated in DES system. A mixture of thymol (HBAs) and menthol (HBDs) has recently been recognized as DES and categorized as type V [23]. Cyclic oligosac- charides (CD) which are non-toxic and obtained from the enzymatic degradation of polysaccharide (starch) were used as HBAs for the production of supramolecular mixtures in the liquid state at room temperature [24, 25]. Furthermore, based on water solubility, DESs have been classified as i) hydrophilic deep eutectic solvents and ii) hydrophobic deep eutectic solvents [26]. The replacement of traditional solvents by DESs as reaction media in synthetic organic [27, 28] and enzymatic reactions [29, 30] has encouraged researchers working in different fields of chemical analyses including preparative chromatography for successful appli- cations of DES. ## 2 Solvent polarity Some unique characteristics of DESs including their ability of solubilizing compounds with different polarities, the capability to tune polarity as per requirement and efficacy of improving solubility of selected compounds have encouraged researchers to use eutectic solvents as alluring

alternatives to traditional organic solvents. The polarity of a solvent is an important parameter which plays an important role in separation science, specifically in chromatographic separation techniques. Semi-empirical linear free energy relationships have been used to characterize the polarity of solvents. # 4 Applications of DESs in different chromatographic technologies Since a long time, organic volatile solvents have been utilized in many types of chromatographic techniques. However, the high cost, enormous consumption and waste generation have a negative impact on human health and even cause pollution in the environment. As a result, these volatile solvents have been replaced by environmentally benign green solvents such as water, supercritical fluid (SCF), ILs and DESs. DESs have been recommended as attractive and highly performing green solvent systems in terms of sensitivity, selectivity and precision for researchers in almost all types of chromatographic methods as a mobile phase additive/component, stationary phase impregnant/modifier and stationary phase materials.

In fact, the DESs-containing mobile phases have shown improved separation efficacy. However, several issues which need to be resolved before using DESs in LC include: (i) high viscous nature which restricts the easy flow of mobile phase through stationary phase material packed in column or spread over TLC plate, (ii) strong inter-linking with stationary phases which affects separation performance efficiencies leading to the shortening of column life, (iii) lack of availability of the high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) grade DESs and (iv) low volatility of DESs which can have negative effects on detector systems. Due to these drawbacks, DESs have not been proven to be as suitable mobile phase solvents as they deserve for chromatography. Natural DESs, on the other hand, have been discovered to be possible optional solvents in liquid chromatography [56]. They focused on future research and concluded that the development of relevant technologies is required before natural DESs may be utilized in HPLC analysis. These advancements include
high-temperature endurable instrument, an improved pump system to provide high back pressure and stationary phases that allow chromatographic analysis at a high temperature to reduce DESs viscosity.

## 4.1 Gas chromatography (GC) Boczkaj et al. [57] first employed DESs as stationary phases in gas chromatography. The stationary phase comprised of a mixture of heptadecanoic acid (HDC) as HBD (melting point of 61.3 °C) and tetrabutylammonium chloride (TBAC) as HBA (melting point of 70 °C) in 2:1 molar ratio and was found to be appropriate for the resolution of volatile organic compounds (VOC). The selectivity efficacy of DES-based synthesized stationary phase for large number of organic compounds (alcohols, ketones, thiophenes and aromatic hydrocarbons) was determined and compared with the selectivity pattern of commercially available GC stationary phases utilizing the values of the Rohrschneider–McReynolds constants [58–61] as shown in Tables 5 and 6, respectively. The Rohrschneider–McReynolds constants indicate that the synthesized DES was the stationary phase of medium polarity. However, the newly synthesized stationary phase with DES has strong interactions with alcohols, because of (i) intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the DES component (HBD and HBA) and the –OH group of alcohols, and (ii) hydrophobic interactions of the DES with the alkyl chains of alcohols, while retention increases significantly with carbon chain length. In comparison to other alcohols, n-hexyl alcohol and n-heptyl alcohol were found to have higher retention. As a result, the retention periods of these two alcohols are by 191% and 300% longer, respectively, than the expected values based on their boiling points. The findings of this study expand the range of applications for DESs by allowing them to be used as sorptive media in chromatographic procedures. The properties of DESs can be modified by either changing one of its components or adding solute dissolved in DES attributed to a lot of possibilities for developing new stationary phases. The retention data presented in Table 5 suggest that these might be applied for other separation techniques (e.g., extractive distillation).

The following parameters mainly affect the resolution of IQAs as discussed below.

i. Nature of stationary phase: This is the most important parameter which mainly impacts the chromatographic behaviour of IQAs in SFC analysis. Different stationary phases like Agilent Zorbax (SB-C18, RX-SIL and Eclipse XDB-C8) columns along with Thermo Scientific Syncronis Amino column were used to optimize the peak shapes and resolution of IQAs [63]. Among these, Zorbax RX-SIL column gave satisfactory results with good peak shapes for the IQAs compared to the other reversed-phase columns. It was probably due to the high content of silica (≥99.99%) in the column material which resulted in reducing peak tailing via reduction in the silanol effect. Moreover, the separation of basic compounds like IQAs with different structures was difficult on the fully hydroxylated column and other reversed-phase columns. ii. Mobile phase additives: Mobile phase additives play an important role in reducing the magnitude of active silanol groups on the silica surface because the modifier competed with the analytes for HBD/HBA sites on stationary phase surface [64]. Separation of IQAs with methanol containing mixed solvents in the absence of DES was not possible. However, improved separations of all IQAs were found when 0.25% ChCl–Gly (1:2) was used as the modifier. As a result, the mobile phase composed of MeOH–2% H2O–0.5% FA–0.25% ChCl–Gly was found the best for the better resolution of IQAs compared to other mobile phase systems. It happened due to the combined effect of HBDs and HBAs [65]. The hydrogen bonding among free silanol groups on the silica surface and DESs attributed to the improved resolution of IQAs. iii. JPC - Journal of Planar Chromatography - Modern TLC (2022) 35:549-570 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00764-022-00216-x REVIEW <::logo: [Unknown] Check for updates A grey button with a circular arrow icon.::> Development and applications of deep eutectic solvents in different chromatographic techniques Mohammad Faraz Ahmer¹ · Qasim Ullah² Received: 27 September 2022 / Accepted: 5 December 2022 / Published online: 9 January 2023 © Akadémiai Kiadó, Budapest, Hungary 2023 **Abstract** Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) being inexpensive, easy to prepare, biocompatible, biodegradable and environmentally benign have aroused as the most propitious greener solvents for designing novel analytical methods of chemical analysis specially covering almost major fields of chromatography. This review article is majorly concerned with the analytical evaluation of DESs as new generation solvents for use as (a) modifier of silica gel surface via silylation reaction to create new stationary phases, (b) mobile phase (or developer) in liquid chromatography and (c) mobile phase additive to improve chromatographic performance. The sequential evolution of DESs has been briefly presented in tabular form since their beginning from the development of choline chloride/urea eutectic mixture in 2003. It has been observed that three more important properties (ionic conductivity, polarity and viscosity) of DESs can be adjusted to the desired level by proper selection of molar composition of hydrogen bond donor and hydrogen bond acceptor and water content. In this review, we present the recent applications of DESs in chromatography covering the period of the last two decades for assessing their suitability as a new class of green solvents. **Keywords** Deep eutectic solvents · Supercritical fluid chromatography · Counter-current chromatography · Gas chromatography · Capillary electrochromatography · Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) # 1 Introduction Organic solvents are volatile and produce a lot of waste, which would be detrimental to the environment and human health. Organic solvents are being replaced by green or less toxic solvents, for example, ILs (ionic liquids) and DESs (deep eutectic solvents) in separation science particularly in chromatography, in the twenty-first century, based on twelve principles of green chemistry. *Abbott et al.* [1] were the first to prepare the deep eutectic phenomenon in the year of 2003. These workers blended urea and choline chloride having melting points of 133 °C and 302 °C, respectively, in the molar ratio of 1:2 to obtain an eutectic mixture (melting Qasim Ullah *drqasimullah@gmail.com; drqasimullah@manuu.edu.in 1 Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Mewat Engineering College, Gurugram University, Nuh, Haryana, India 2 Physical Sciences Section, School of Sciences, Maulana Azad National Urdu University, Hyderabad, TS 500032, India point: 12 °C) that was liquid at room temperature. Because of alike physical and chemical properties to ILs, DESs were classed as sub-group of ILs. Furthermore, DESs are preferred over ILs as solvents because of their ease of pro- duction, biocompatibility, biodegradability, cost-effective starting materials and low toxicity. Because one of the com- ponents is of natural origin, _Choi et al._ [2] coined the term natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) for DESs. Amino acids, sugars, organic acids, terpenes and phenolic chemi- cals are just a few examples of primary metabolites used to prepare NADES. Since the first report, NADES have been used as an extraction medium particularly for polyphenolics. Table 1 shows the evolution of DESs throughout the history [3]. The commonly used hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) taken together in various molar ratios for the synthesis of numerous eutectic mix- tures are shown in Fig. 1a and b. According to the litera- ture survey, only a few review articles have appeared on the applications of DESs in chromatography [4–6]. _Lenca and_ coworkers have published an admirable review in 2017 on the applications of room-temperature ionic liquids in liquid chromatography [7]. <::logo: Springer Springer Black outline of a chess knight next to the word "Springer".::> 550 JPC – Journal of Planar Chromatography – Modern TLC (2022) 35:549–570 Table 1 Summary of chronological development of deep eutectic solvents (DESs) [3]

According to the literature review, DESs have been widely employed in different analytical applications including separation techniques. A review on the application of green solvents in thin-layer chromatography (TLC) was recently published by Qasim Ullah et al. [8]. Furthermore, in recent years, DESs have received more attention of researchers, resulting in the arising number of studies appearing in the literature about properties [9–12] and their applications [13–21]. Abbott and coworkers [22] categorized DESs into four groups based on their compositional components as shown in Fig. 2. According to the literature survey, type III DESs analogs to ILs in terms of physicochemical properties have been commonly investigated in DES system. A mixture of thymol (HBAs) and menthol (HBDs) has recently been recognized as DES and categorized as type V [23]. However, the high cost, enormous consumption and waste generation have a negative impact on human health and even cause pollution in the environment. As a result, these volatile solvents have been replaced by environmentally benign green solvents such as water, supercritical fluid (SCF), ILs and DESs. DESs have been recommended as attractive and highly performing green solvent systems in terms of sensitivity, selectivity and precision for researchers in almost all types of chromatographic methods as a mobile phase additive/component, stationary phase impregnant/modifier and stationary phase materials. In fact, the DESs-containing mobile phases have shown improved separation efficacy. However, several issues which need to be resolved before using DESs in LC include: (i) high viscous nature which restricts the easy flow of mobile phase through stationary phase material packed in column or spread over TLC plate, (ii) strong inter-linking with stationary phases which affects separation performance efficiencies leading to the shortening of column life, (iii) lack of availability of the high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) grade DESs and (iv) low volatility of DESs which can have negative effects on detector systems. Due to these drawbacks, DESs have not been proven to be as suitable mobile phase solvents as they deserve for chromatography. Natural DESs, on the other hand, have been discovered to be possible optional solvents in liquid chromatography [56]. They focused on future research and concluded that the development of relevant technologies is required before natural DESs may be utilized in HPLC analysis. These advancements include high-temperature endurable instrument, an improved pump system to provide high back pressure and stationary phases that allow chromatographic analysis at a high temperature to reduce DESs viscosity. ## 4.1 Gas chromatography (GC) Boczkaj et al. [57] first employed DESs as stationary phases in gas chromatography. The stationary phase comprised of a mixture of heptadecanoic acid (HDC) as HBD (melting point of 61.3 °C) and tetrabutylammonium chloride (TBAC) as HBA (melting point of 70 °C) in 2:1 molar ratio and was found to be appropriate for the resolution of volatile organic compounds (VOC). The selectivity efficacy of DES-based synthesized stationary phase for large number of organic compounds (alcohols, ketones, thiophenes and aromatic hydrocarbons) was determined and compared with the selectivity pattern of commercially available GC stationary phases utilizing the values of the Rohrschneider–McReynolds constants [58–61] as shown in Tables 5 and 6, respectively. The Rohrschneider–McReynolds constants indicate that the synthesized DES was the stationary phase of medium polarity. However, the newly synthesized stationary phase with DES has strong interactions with alcohols, because of (i) intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the DES component (HBD and HBA) and the –OH group of alcohols, and (ii) hydrophobic interactions of the DES with the alkyl chains of alcohols, while retention increases significantly with carbon chain length. In comparison to other alcohols, n-hexyl alcohol and n-heptyl alcohol were found to have higher retention. As a result, the retention periods of these two alcohols are by 191% and 300% longer, respectively, than the expected values based on their boiling points. The findings of this study expand the range of applications for DESs by allowing them to be used as sorptive media in chromatographic procedures. The properties of DESs can be modified by either changing one of its components or adding solute dissolved in DES attributed to a lot of possibilities for developing new stationary phases. The retention data presented in Table 5 suggest that these might be applied for other separation techniques (e.g., extractive distillation). This review article is majorly concerned with the analytical evaluation of DESs as new generation solvents for use as (a) modifier of silica gel surface via silylation reaction to create new stationary phases, (b) mobile phase (or developer) in liquid chromatography and (c) mobile phase additive to improve chromatographic performance. The sequential evolution of DESs has been briefly presented in tabular form since their beginning from the development of choline chloride/urea eutectic mixture in 2003. It has been observed that three more important properties (ionic conductivity, polarity and viscosity) of DESs can be adjusted to the desired level by proper selection of molar composition of hydrogen bond donor and hydrogen bond acceptor and water content. In this review, we present the recent applications of DESs in chromatography covering the period of the last two decades for assessing their suitability as a new class of green solvents. **Keywords** Deep eutectic solvents · Supercritical fluid chromatography · Counter-current chromatography · Gas chromatography · Capillary electrochromatography · Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) # 1 Introduction Organic solvents are volatile and produce a lot of waste, which would be detrimental to the environment and human health. Organic solvents are being replaced by green or less toxic solvents, for example, ILs (ionic liquids) and DESs (deep eutectic solvents) in separation science particularly in chromatography, in the twenty-first century, based on twelve principles of green chemistry. *Abbott et al.* [1] were the first to prepare the deep eutectic phenomenon in the year of 2003. Because one of the com- ponents is of natural origin, _Choi et al._ [2] coined the term natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES) for DESs. According to the literature review, DESs have been widely employed in different analytical applications including separation techniques. A review on the application of green solvents in thin-layer chromatography (TLC) was recently published by Qasim Ullah et al. [8]. Furthermore, in recent years, DESs have received more attention of researchers, resulting in the arising number of studies appearing in the literature about properties [9–12] and their applications [13–21]. Abbott and coworkers [22] categorized DESs into four groups based on their compositional components as shown in Fig. 2. According to the literature survey, type III DESs analogs to ILs in terms of physicochemical properties have been commonly investigated in DES system. A mixture of thymol (HBAs) and menthol (HBDs) has recently been recognized as DES and categorized as type V [23]. Cyclic oligosac- charides (CD) which are non-toxic and obtained from the enzymatic degradation of polysaccharide (starch) were used as HBAs for the production of supramolecular mixtures in the liquid state at room temperature [24, 25]. Furthermore, based on water solubility, DESs have been classified as i) hydrophilic deep eutectic solvents and ii) hydrophobic deep eutectic solvents [26]. The replacement of traditional solvents by DESs as reaction media in synthetic organic [27, 28] and enzymatic reactions [29, 30] has encouraged researchers working in different fields of chemical analyses including preparative chromatography for successful appli- cations of DES. [Tables 7, 8, 9]. ## 2 Solvent polarity Some unique characteristics of DESs including their ability of solubilizing compounds with different polarities, the capability to tune polarity as per requirement and efficacy of improving solubility of selected compounds have encouraged researchers to use eutectic solvents as alluring alternatives to traditional organic solvents. The polarity of a solvent is an important parameter which plays an important role in separation science, specifically in chromatographic separation techniques. Semi-empirical linear free energy relationships have been used to characterize the polarity of solvents. However, the high cost, enormous consumption and waste generation have a negative impact on human health and even cause pollution in the environment. As a result, these volatile solvents have been replaced by environmentally benign green solvents such as water, supercritical fluid (SCF), ILs and DESs. DESs have been recommended as attractive and highly performing green solvent systems in terms of sensitivity, selectivity and precision for researchers in almost all types of chromatographic methods as a mobile phase additive/component, stationary phase impregnant/modifier and stationary phase materials. In fact, the DESs-containing mobile phases have shown improved separation efficacy. However, several issues which need to be resolved before using DESs in LC include: (i) high viscous nature which restricts the easy flow of mobile phase through stationary phase material packed in column or spread over TLC plate, (ii) strong inter-linking with stationary phases which affects separation performance efficiencies leading to the shortening of column life, (iii) lack of availability of the high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) grade DESs and (iv) low volatility of DESs which can have negative effects on detector systems. Due to these drawbacks, DESs have not been proven to be as suitable mobile phase solvents as they deserve for chromatography. Natural DESs, on the other hand, have been discovered to be possible optional solvents in liquid chromatography [56]. They focused on future research and concluded that the development of relevant technologies is required before natural DESs may be utilized in HPLC analysis. These advancements include high-temperature endurable instrument, an improved pump system to provide high back pressure and stationary phases that allow chromatographic analysis at a high temperature to reduce DESs viscosity. ## 4.1 Gas chromatography (GC) Boczkaj et al. [57] first employed DESs as stationary phases in gas chromatography. The stationary phase comprised of a mixture of heptadecanoic acid (HDC) as HBD (melting point of 61.3 °C) and tetrabutylammonium chloride (TBAC) as HBA (melting point of 70 °C) in 2:1 molar ratio and was found to be appropriate for the resolution of volatile organic compounds (VOC). The selectivity efficacy of DES-based synthesized stationary phase for large number of organic compounds (alcohols, ketones, thiophenes and aromatic hydrocarbons) was determined and compared with the selectivity pattern of commercially available GC stationary phases utilizing the values of the Rohrschneider–McReynolds constants [58–61] as shown in Tables 5 and 6, respectively. The Rohrschneider–McReynolds constants indicate that the synthesized DES was the stationary phase of medium polarity. However, the newly synthesized stationary phase with DES has strong interactions with alcohols, because of (i) intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the DES component (HBD and HBA) and the –OH group of alcohols, and (ii) hydrophobic interactions of the DES with the alkyl chains of alcohols, while retention increases significantly with carbon chain length. In comparison to other alcohols, n-hexyl alcohol and n-heptyl alcohol were found to have higher retention. As a result, the retention periods of these two alcohols are by 191% and 300% longer, respectively, than the expected values based on their boiling points. The findings of this study expand the range of applications for DESs by allowing them to be used as sorptive media in chromatographic procedures. The properties of DESs can be modified by either changing one of its components or adding solute dissolved in DES attributed to a lot of possibilities for developing new stationary phases. The retention data presented in Table 5 suggest that these might be applied for other separation techniques (e.g., extractive distillation).
